# Records that outrun their witnesses

Whoever relies on an agent-produced record later — an auditor, a
researcher, the producer's own future systems — needs a way to check
it that does not depend on having watched it being made. At the Axiom
Foundation, software agents write three record surfaces this paper
concerns: pre-registered forecasts, an append-only observation ledger,
and statutes encoded as executable rules. People review samples and
deterministic gates decide what merges; no person witnesses every
record at the rate agents produce them.

This paper treats the producer's repositories, CI configuration, key
settings, and self-operated monitoring as non-independent trust
inputs: the producer can reconfigure each of them, so under this
threat model none of them alone can establish custody for an outside
verifier.

The receipt package takes the custody route. The producer writes
verifiable records as it works — chained manifests, timestamp tokens,
signatures, attestations — and a verifier with a clone of the
repository later checks the saved evidence against trust anchors the
verifier committed in its own code. This paper states what those
checks establish (@sec-guarantees), why the design follows from the
threat model (@sec-design), how the machinery earned its way into one
package (@sec-extraction), who adopts it (@sec-adoption), and where it
sits among adjacent systems (@sec-related).

# What a verifier can conclude {#sec-guarantees}

Four checks cover the record surface. The verifier composes them;
each conclusion is conditional on the specification, trust material,
and options the verifier itself supplied, and each check refuses
rather than warns when its evidence falls short [@receipt-repo].

**Append-only history.** The release-chain verifier, run with its
default options, establishes a contiguous, content-addressed,
producer-signed manifest history from genesis to head whose recorded
state matches the working tree. Supplying a trusted base reference
strengthens the conclusion: every release file present at that
ancestor still carries identical bytes and file mode. The append gate
gives its strongest conclusion the same way — with a base reference
and a data-surface change, a candidate tree extends the trusted ledger
exactly: prefix retained, rows valid, releases untouched, and any
ledger append paired with exactly the next release set.

**Witnessed time.** Each accepted RFC 3161 token [@rfc3161]
establishes that the record existed no later than the token's signed
time, under the consumer's timestamp-authority assumptions: the
verifier checks the token cryptographically against the pinned root
certificates, policy identifiers, and signer identities in the
consumer's specification, for every anchor that specification
configures. A witness may record an authority as unavailable with a
reason; the verifier treats that as a verified declaration of
unavailability, never as proof from that authority.

**Producer signatures.** Ed25519 signatures verify against public keys
whose fingerprints live in the verifier's committed specification.
Keyrings support N-of-M thresholds over a domain-separated payload and
explicit legacy generations: callers exclude retired keys for new
material with `allow_legacy=False` and may enable them for immutable
history with `allow_legacy=True`, and malformed or mispinned key
material fails the check outright rather than being skipped in favor
of a sibling key that happens to verify.

**Workflow provenance.** For commits touching a protected tree, the
attestation check establishes that GitHub's attestation service
accepted the canonical subject for that commit under an anchored
workflow identity. This is the package's one networked check — it
calls the GitHub CLI — and callers compose the provided helpers
(protected-history enumeration, enforcement epochs) into a full-history
sweep; the package supplies the pieces, not a single spanning call.

The 0.5.0 changes, open for review as of this writing, propose a fifth
layer [@receipt-pr14]: a closed-world binding between a witnessed
journal and the configured corpus — within the specification's content
roots, an unlisted file, a missing file, a rewritten byte, or a symlink
where a regular file was recorded each refuses — and a spanning
`receipt verify` command that runs custody, binding, and
declaration-completeness passes in order, stopping at the first
failure. Its verdict is fail-closed in the strict sense the proposed
verifier documents: pass only if every stage completed and every
required declaration was found; anything else, including an exception
the verifier did not anticipate, is a failure. The command renders
what it did not establish just as plainly — that any declared gate
actually passed, or that encoded rules read the law correctly.

# Why the shape follows from the threat {#sec-design}

Each design rule answers a specific way verification could quietly
come to depend on the producer.

**Trust anchors live in the verifier's committed code.** Key
fingerprints, timestamp-authority roots, policy identifiers, content
roots, and required declarations sit in a specification the consumer
commits and reviews. The package ships no defaults: no configuration
surface a producer could preload, no environment variable a deployment
could override. The caller always supplies signing keys; the package
neither stores key material nor reads trust configuration from the
environment.

**Rotation is loud.** Replacing a key is a reviewed change to the
consumer's repository that moves the retired key into an explicit
legacy generation, and the caller chooses per call whether legacy
generations may vouch at all. There are no time-based transition
windows in which either key silently works.

**Verification of saved evidence runs offline on commodity tools.** A
clone, Python, OpenSSL, and Git suffice for the chain, time, and
signature checks, so they work against a producer whose infrastructure
is unavailable — or untrustworthy — at verification time. The
workflow-attestation check is the explicit exception: it queries
GitHub, and the package's differential evidence for that surface is
scoped accordingly (@sec-extraction).

**Specified gaps refuse.** Missing witnesses, malformed rows, unknown
keys, out-of-range times, unlistable directories, paths that escape
the configured roots: the verifiers refuse each with a typed error.
On the ported surfaces the refusal text is the production system's
own, preserved through extraction; the proposed corpus surface ships a
new refusal battery with the same posture. The libraries own no
stdout or stderr; callers render acceptance and refusal, and exit
codes carry the verdict.

# The machinery {#sec-machinery}

Together the six modules shipping in 0.4.0 verify a record set's
history, timing, and authorship from saved evidence; the API reference
at [axiom.org/receipt/api](https://axiom.org/receipt/api/) documents
their public interfaces.

| Module | A pass establishes |
|---|---|
| `canonical` | One byte stream per value: canonical JSON with UTF-16 code-unit key order and ECMAScript number formatting, byte-compatible with the producer's TypeScript implementation. |
| `release_chain` | With default options: a contiguous, content-addressed, producer-signed, witness-receipted manifest history matching recorded state; with a trusted base reference: byte-and-mode immutability of all published release files since that ancestor. |
| `append_gate` | With a base reference and a data-surface change: a candidate tree extends the trusted ledger exactly — prefix retained, rows valid, releases untouched, appends paired with exactly the next release set. Without a base reference, full-file invariants only. |
| `sign` | Raw Ed25519 signatures over exact bytes; N-of-M thresholds over a domain-separated payload under consumer-pinned keyrings, with legacy generations governed by the caller's `allow_legacy` choice. |
| `tsa` | One RFC 3161 token matches one consumer-pinned anchor — root bytes, policy, imprint, signed time, signer identity — via OpenSSL; witness sidecars follow the trust-bundle transition rules. |
| `attest` | GitHub's attestation service accepted the canonical subject for a commit under an anchored workflow identity; helpers enumerate protected-tree history and its enforcement epoch for callers to compose. |

The open 0.5.0 review adds `corpus` (the closed-world journal binding
and gate-declaration parsing), `verify` (the spanning pass ordering),
and `cli` (`receipt verify`, with text and JSON rendering and
meaningful exit codes) [@receipt-pr14].

# How the machinery earned its way in {#sec-extraction}

Three production systems built this machinery before the package
existed: pre-registered forecast records [@brier-repo], an observation
ledger's release chain [@ledger-repo], and a signed statute corpus
[@axiom-corpus-431]. The forecast and ledger systems supplied verifier
surfaces; the statute corpus supplied key-rotation semantics that the
package adapted and tested. Extraction, rather than reimplementation,
preserved what the harnesses could hold it to: on the ported surfaces,
the refusal behavior of verifiers that had already caught real
mistakes in production, to the extent the differential batteries
exercise it. Four evidence classes cover everything in the package,
and the evidence for each class is published.

**Byte-identical port.** The canonical-JSON module is the ledger's
file, verbatim: a test pins its SHA-256 against the recorded upstream
hash, so equivalence is identity.

**Differential extraction against the unmodified source verifier.**
The release-chain and append-gate surfaces (from the ledger) and the
witness and attestation surfaces (from the forecast system) came
across behind differential harnesses. Each harness pins the upstream
source files by SHA-256, runs the unmodified upstream verifier as an
oracle on live production fixtures — the forecast fixture carries 53
snapshots, 52 available witnesses, and 91 real timestamp tokens — and
requires the package to reproduce the oracle's verdicts, accepted and
refused alike, down to message bytes after two disclosed
normalizations (surrounding whitespace and volatile OpenSSL
error-queue identifiers). At the current review head the four
harnesses run 94 cases, all passing.^[Local run at commit `c711adc`,
2026-08-10: 36 release-chain, 21 append-gate, 17 witness, and 20
attestation differential tests. The attestation harness compares
command construction and outcome handling against a local `gh` stub
and claims no live-network equivalence; the witness harness documents
its exclusions in the test file.] The extraction-time record is also
published: the 633-line, 42-hunk release-chain port diff drew three
independent review passes — two requesting changes, then approval —
and the 695-line append-gate diff a separate approving review that
sabotaged base-tree materialization and watched 4 of 17 differential
cases fail, evidence that the harness binds the base-tree behavior it
claims to bind [@receipt-receipts].

**Semantic adaptation of a production incident.** The signing module's
legacy-generation semantics come from the statute corpus, which
learned them the expensive way: rotating a release key had made
previously published, immutable releases unverifiable
[@axiom-corpus-431]. The fix — retired keys keep verifying the history
they signed, only the current generation signs anything new, malformed
key material is always fatal — entered the package as a design
adaptation with direct tests and no differential oracle.

**New composition.** The proposed corpus binding, spanning verifier,
and CLI are new code composed from the extracted parts. They add no
cryptography and no trust anchors of their own; their evidence is a
refusal battery over the closed-world binding rules [@receipt-pr14].

The published evidence is uneven in exactly the way the classes
predict, and the repository states which is which: the ledger lane has
raw port diffs, pinned hashes, and independent static reviews; the
forecast lane has pinned hashes and maintained differential harnesses
but no raw port diff; the rotation semantics trace through the pull
requests that carried them (receipt's own and the corpus incident's
[@axiom-corpus-431]) rather than a receipts-directory artifact.

# Adoption {#sec-adoption}

As of August 11, 2026, three codebases pin released versions of the
package and call it from their verification paths: the Axiom encoder
delegates its apply-manifest verification to the package's threshold
keyring check on its default branch; the forecast system's verifier
and signer import the package's signature primitives under a custody
extra on its default branch; and the observation ledger's custody
branch replaces its local verifier and append gate with thin shims
over the package, with the differential harnesses re-run on every
package change. Dependency pins and call sites are checkable in each
repository; this paper claims code-level adoption, and the receipt
repository separately states that the ledger consumes the package in
production.

The open corpus-verification pull requests propose extending the same
custody discipline to a published rule corpus. The New Zealand pilot
commits a verification specification — custody key, two
timestamp-authority anchors, content roots, required declarations —
and a witnessed journal of 104 rows binding 80 content files, 7
attested paths, and 17 gate declarations, so an outside auditor could
run one offline command over a clone and get a fail-closed verdict
[@rulespec-nz-104]. Gate rows are declarations: the proposed verifier
proves they were made and bound, and states plainly that it did not
rerun them.

# Related systems {#sec-related}

receipt assembles per-consumer custody policy in committed code,
multi-anchor timestamp composition, record-level history checks, and
(in the open 0.5.0 review) closed-world corpus binding under one
fail-closed verdict that names its non-conclusions. Each neighboring
system solves an adjacent problem, and several share individual
features; the differences below are checkable against their
specifications.

RFC 3161 timestamping [@rfc3161] defines the single-token transaction
receipt builds on; the package composes saved tokens from the
consumer's configured authorities with pinned roots, policies, and
signer identities, verified offline from the saved evidence.
Certificate Transparency [@rfc9162] puts TLS certificates in public
append-only logs with third-party monitors; receipt verifies a
repository-local history against consumer pins without a log service,
accepting the narrower scope in exchange for no trusted log operator.
The Update Framework [@tuf-spec; @Samuel2010Survivable] also roots
trust client-side and supports thresholds and offline root keys, but
is an updater protocol for fetching current metadata; receipt checks
an already obtained clone's history and rotates roots only through the
consumer's reviewed specification. Sigstore's default keyless flow
[@Newman2022Sigstore] binds signatures to OIDC identities via
short-lived certificates and a transparency log, its bundles verify
offline, and it also supports self-managed keys and custom deployments;
receipt uses no identity federation and no log in any configuration,
pinning producer and authority identities directly in each consumer's
specification. in-toto [@TorresArias2019InToto] verifies that
supply-chain steps matched an owner-signed layout, records the
materials and products passed to its tooling, and derives its coverage
from the authored layout rules; receipt verifies custody of the
records themselves and treats process gates strictly as declarations
it never reruns. SLSA [@slsa-spec] specifies leveled requirements for
build and source integrity rather than mandating one verifier; receipt
is a concrete verifier a consumer points at one history. Reproducible
builds [@reproducible-builds] compare independently rebuilt artifacts
byte for byte; receipt's differential harnesses compare verifier
verdicts on common fixtures, a related but distinct discipline. Signed
Git commits [@gitformat-signature] authenticate commit objects under
locally configured trust — including a repository-relative allowed-
signers file, so local trust configuration is not unique to receipt;
receipt additionally verifies the domain-specific chain, witnessed
time, historical file bytes and modes, and (proposed) corpus binding.

# Scope and pending work {#sec-scope}

A pass establishes custody, not truth: the verifier recognizes gate
declarations but does not rerun them, and nothing in a verdict says
encoded rules read the law correctly. An honestly witnessed stale
clone can pass; a base reference adds immutability relative to the
specified ancestor, and freshness requires an out-of-band expectation.
Consumers configure timestamp-authority diversity; the verifier
enforces the configured anchor set and cannot prove that authorities
fail independently. The differential harnesses cover finite fixture
and mutation batteries — each test file documents its commands, source
pins, and exclusions, which is also the rerun recipe — not all
possible inputs, and the package inherits the standard assumptions of
its primitives: signature schemes and hash functions unbroken,
timestamp authorities honest about time, certificate material valid at
verification time. Key compromise before rotation, and an equivocating
producer who maintains parallel histories for different verifiers,
sit outside what a single clone's custody check can detect. The
waiver ratchet and chronology tiers remain in their source systems
pending extraction, and the spanning CLI is part of the open 0.5.0
review. The package is Python; producers on other stacks interoperate
at the artifact layer (canonical JSON, manifests, tokens, signatures)
rather than the library layer.

# Availability

`receipt` is on PyPI (Apache-2.0), with source, port diffs, review
records, and differential harnesses at
[github.com/TheAxiomFoundation/receipt](https://github.com/TheAxiomFoundation/receipt),
the package page at [axiom.org/receipt](https://axiom.org/receipt),
and the API reference at
[axiom.org/receipt/api](https://axiom.org/receipt/api/).
